item.title: Extending building longevity: wood-based product–service systems
item.description:
Wood has been considered renewable, low-carbon and flexible for use in buildings. Product–service system (PSS) configurations related to building longevity are identified by using PSS archetypes as analytical lenses. These PSS configurations of buildings containing wood are assessed against resource efficiency (RE) and circular economy (CE) hierarchies. Qualitative interviews (n = 31) from Finland provide insights into opportunities for timber products in the building sector. The use of timber in construction and retrofit innovations is examined for flexibility and extending building lifespans. Lower-level practices from CE hierarchies (e.g. material recycling) appeared more institutionalised while higher-level practices from RE hierarchy (e.g. use of vacant spaces) seemed to be more in their early stages. As a response to the expected market growth, innovation bundles were found to centre around new construction, lacking a needed emphasis shift to sharing spaces and building retrofits.

PRACTICE RELEVANCE

This study makes a case for stronger integration of PSS thinking into timber construction and retrofits. Developing such solutions requires greater co-creation with multiple stakeholders involved during the building life-cycle, including the integration of end-user and living phase aspects into building planning. Future legislation and policy could support this development at the national and city policy levels by encouraging renovation, adaptability and incorporation of services that extend building longevity.

item.title: Capturing circular value for building sector actors
item.description:
Environmental and life-cycle cost assessments of two renovation case studies in Montreal, Canada—a single-detached house and a triplex—investigated three different renovation scenarios: business-as-usual, recycling, and reuse. Results indicate that incorporating circular reuse principles offers the highest potential to reduce environmental impacts while lowering costs. Higher upfront costs and labour requirements for selective deconstruction are subsequently offset by savings via the use of secondary materials. As contractors typically prioritise initial budget considerations within project-based delivery frameworks, these redistributed gains may remain insufficiently visible at the decision-making stage, leaving longer term economic and environmental benefits partially obscured for contractors and clients. A structural mismatch exists between academic evaluations (often framed from cradle to cradle) and industry perspectives focused on project completion. Addressing this misalignment requires rethinking how value is assessed in the building sector, moving beyond upfront costs towards incorporating longer term environmental and economic considerations. By grounding life-cycle assessments in real renovation contexts and translating them into contractor-focused guidance, this study contributes practice-based evidence to support circular renovation decision-making and policy discussions.

PRACTICE RELEVANCE

This study outlines how circular renovation of a single-detached house and a triplex can achieve economic and environmental reductions if fully implemented. This includes a two-phase construction process: phase 1 (selective deconstruction) and phase 2 (renovation with secondary materials). If only phase 1 is followed, costs for the project rise as this phase is more costly than demolition. However, when both construction phases are followed, net negative greenhouse gas emissions can be achieved, representing a 123% reduction relative to a linear renovation (demolition and the use of primary materials). This significant reduction is due to the avoided burden approach which generates environmental credits that exceed gross impacts, resulting in negative net emissions. Project costs can also be reduced by up to 19%. A deconstruction guide produced for contractors showcases the best practices in selective deconstruction and reuse, and highlights the potential environmental and economic savings.

item.title: Summertime overheating in apartments with glazed balconies: a Finnish study
item.description:
Apartment overheating is increasingly an issue due to rising global temperatures, likely exceeding 2°C in Finland over the next few decades. This overlooked issue in Nordic housing is exacerbated by building characteristics ill-suited to keeping cool indoor environments, such as lack of solar shading or large operable windows and the use of glazed balconies. However, there is limited empirical evidence on summertime overheating in glazed-balcony apartments in the Nordic climate. To bridge this gap, this exploratory case-study investigation assessed summertime overheating in 10 apartments with glazed balconies in Finland during the summer of 2025 and investigated how occupant behaviour affected overheating risk. In-situ temperature measurements were collected in the balcony and apartment spaces alongside semi-structured interviews and balcony-use diaries. Findings highlighted that apartments built to the current Finnish building code failed to meet overheating criteria, and the presence of a glazed balcony was one of several variables linked to apartment overheating. Glazed balconies became uncomfortably hot for extended periods, limiting the intended year-round usability. Moreover, the balcony door was often the apartment’s sole purge ventilation route and was found to be ineffective. These findings are increasingly relevant internationally as glazed balcony solutions are gaining adoption in other contexts.

PRACTICE RELEVANCE

There is a pressing need to implement overheating mitigation strategies for glazed balconies, as well as the apartment more generally, to reduce associated risks. Designers and manufacturers must provide robust balcony-glazing solutions with proven operability that support pet-safe intensive ventilation, shading, furniture placement and everyday usability. Apartment window systems outside of the glazed balcony should also enable large and safe openings for effective natural ventilation. Indirect factors to be considered include: (1) updating regulatory climate datasets to consider current and future climate scenarios; (2) the balcony glazing should systematically be drawn with ‘glazing fully open’ as the default state during design ensuring usability in this condition; and (3) occupant behaviour should be supported through explicit guidance, including recommending to fully open balcony glazing during warm periods.
